needs.definition: A day inside a power window on which the household has no working electric light after sunset: its ordinary flashlights, phone torches and candles are dead, used up or cannot be found. Charged per person. Meeting it takes about 4 Wh of LED light per household-day (one or two lamps at ~1 W for 4-5 dark waking hours).

baselineCoverageDays.basis: 94.8% of households said they had a working flashlight and batteries (CDC BRFSS, 14 states, 2006-2010, https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6136a1.htm) and 91% of adults own a smartphone with a torch (Pew 2025, search snippet). The day count is my guess: one flashlight with part-used cells gives 5-20 h, i.e. 1-4 evenings; phone torches compete with calls.

hardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: Stated WTP to avoid a 24 h outage is $53.68 per household (LBNL ICE 2.0, https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf) and FEMA uses $33 per person-day; I assign 15-25% of that to light, about $10 per household-evening, divided by 2.5 persons. No study isolates lighting.

mortalityMicromortsPerPersonDay.basis: Data: about 3,700 unintentional fall deaths at ages 15-59 in 2023 (WISQARS: 332 at 25-34, 677 at 35-44, 1,250 at 45-54, 3,172 at 55-64, https://wisqars-viz.cdc.gov/pdfs/leading-causes-of-injury-deaths-by-age-group_2023_508.pdf) among roughly 197M people = 1.9 per 100,000 a year = 0.052 micromorts a day. Falls and fractures among over-65s rose 40% in New Jersey in the week after Sandy (https://medicalxpress.com/news/2013-11-falls-fractures-elderly-superstorm-sandy.html) in a population that mostly owned flashlights. Judgement: having no light at all adds 35% (8-100%) of daily fall risk over having battery light. 0.052 x 0.35 = 0.018.

multipliers.basis: Fall deaths 19.2 per 100,000 at 65-74 (NCHS Data Brief 532, 2023, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db532.htm) and about 9 at 60-64 (half of the 3,172 deaths at 55-64, WISQARS) give 15.3 for 60-74 = 0.42 micromorts a day, eight times the 0.052 base rate. Hardship: slower dark adaptation, guess.

Fall deaths 74.7 (75-84) and 339.5 (85+) per 100,000 in 2023 (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db532.htm) = 141.5 for 75+ = 3.88 micromorts a day, 75 times the 0.052 base rate; x0.35 = 1.36 micromorts per dark day. Hardship adds non-fatal fall injury, guess.
No rate found for this group below age 60; assumed several times the base because transfers and toilet trips in the dark are the classic fall setting.
Children rarely die of falls at home; fear of the dark raises hardship.

needs.notes: The mortality figure is the excess of no light over battery light. Outages raise fall risk even in lit homes (Irma: 13 of 129 deaths were falls from standing height in elderly people, https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/mm6730a5.htm), so a light does not remove all outage fall risk. Texas 2021 falls (9 of 246) were on ice, not darkness. Candles meet the need but carry a fire side risk owned by another researcher.

needs.definition: A day inside a power window on which the household has no charged phone and no way to charge one or to run small USB devices. Charged per person. Assumed energy: 15 Wh of rated battery capacity per person-day (about 10 Wh into the phone, two thirds of a ~15 Wh phone battery under rationed use), so about 40 Wh per household-day for 2.5 people including a few Wh for lamps and a radio.

baselineCoverageDays.basis: For a household without a car: a phone lasts about a day in normal use and two in low-power mode; a laptop (50-70 Wh) holds 3-4 phone charges. Households with a car can charge indefinitely from its USB port or 12 V socket while fuel lasts; see openQuestions.

hardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: No direct WTP study found. Whole-outage WTP is $54 per household-day (LBNL ICE 2.0, https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf) and $43-60 a day for partial backup in a 10-day blackout (Baik et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-0581-1); I give phones and small devices about a third of that once they are dead, rising as coordination, work and payments suffer. Applies only while the mobile network is up.

mortalityMicromortsPerPersonDay.basis: Cost of being unable to phone for an ambulance. EMS-treated cardiac arrest is about 0.1% of people a year with ~10% survival (recalled AHA figures), worth ~0.3 micromorts a day on average and ~0.06 for a healthy adult under 60; other time-critical emergencies roughly triple that to 0.2. A dead phone loses perhaps 15% (3-40%) of the benefit, because neighbours, landlines and cars remain: 0.2 x 0.15 = 0.03.

multipliers.basis: Cardiac arrest and other emergencies are roughly 10-20 times more frequent than in adults under 60; EMS benefit 3-4 micromorts a day x 15%.

Must be able to call for help or resupply when a device fails; 15% of Texans surveyed in 2021 said an outage harmed a relative who depends on powered medical equipment (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf).
Needs to reach a pharmacy or prescriber.
Cannot easily walk to a neighbour or drive for help.

needs.notes: Overlaps with the information need (radio), owned by another researcher: do not also count news access here. If the comms window is active the phone is useless and this need should not be charged.

needs.definition: A one-off loss, not a daily one. An unmet day is a day on which fridge or freezer contents pass their safe holding time and are thrown out or eaten at risk. Charged per person (household loss divided by 2.5). Day 1 is the fridge, day 2 the freezer; later days carry only the inconvenience of having no cold storage. Running a fridge-freezer takes about 1,300 Wh a day and a start-up surge of 600-1,200 W.

baselineCoverageDays.basis: Official safe time is 4 h for a closed fridge, 48 h for a full freezer and 24 h for a half-full one (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/keep-food-safe-after-emergency.html). Real losses start later: 4.9M US households reported spoiled food in 2023 (AHS, https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/10/power-outages.html), about the 4.6M (3.5% of 131M) that NREL data imply had an outage over 24 h (https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy23osti/83092.pdf), though 23.6M had one of 6 h or more. So median practical coverage is about 10 h.

hardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: Household loss: fridge $45 (15-130), freezer $110 (30-350), total about $155; divided by 2.5. Anchors: Con Edison pays up to $280 on an itemised list and $655 with proof (https://www.coned.com/en/services-and-outages/claim-form/residential-spoilage-claim-form); marketing surveys put the loss at $117-200 an outage (search snippets, unverified); only 31% discard fridge food and 37% thawed frozen food (RTI 2011, https://rti.org/news/most-americans-are-not-prepared-ensure-food-safety-during-power-outages), which is why the expected fridge loss is below the value of the contents. Day 3 onward: $5 per household-day for shopping daily and eating shelf food, guess.

mortalityMicromortsPerPersonDay.basis: Foodborne illness kills about 3,000 Americans a year (recalled CDC estimate) = 0.025 micromorts per person-day, mostly the old and immunocompromised; perhaps 0.005 for a healthy adult. Diarrhoeal illness rose after the 2003 New York blackout and was tied to meat (OR 2.7) and seafood (OR 4.8) eaten afterwards (Marx et al. 2006, search snippet). I assume risk triples on the days spoiled food is still being eaten.

multipliers.basis: Higher case fatality from foodborne infection.
Foodborne deaths concentrate in the oldest.

Refrigerated drugs. 705,000 households, 2.9% of those holding refrigerated medicine, reported spoiled medicine in 2023 against 14% of outage households reporting spoiled food (AHS, https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/10/power-outages.html). Insulin, opened or not, keeps working for up to 28 days at 59-86F (FDA, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/emergency-preparedness-drugs/information-regarding-insulin-storage-and-switching-between-products-emergency), so short outages cost money and worry, not health; multipliers are a guess.

needs.notes: Insulin and similar drugs: nothing happens in an outage under four weeks unless the home is hotter than 86F (30C); above that potency falls gradually and FDA says keep using it until replaced. A Cochrane review (2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37930742/, abstract snippet only) found unopened human insulin holds up to six months at 25C and two months at 37C. Biologics and GLP-1 pens have shorter room-temperature limits (often 14 days; recalled, unverified) and cost far more to replace. In a winter outage the need mostly disappears because food can go outdoors (15% did so, RTI).

needs.definition: A person-day without a powered medical device, for a person who depends on one, after the device's own battery and any backup cylinders have run out. The base curve is for an IMPORTANT but not life-supporting device (CPAP or BiPAP for sleep apnoea, nebuliser, feeding pump, powered wheelchair). It is zero for people with no device and must not be applied to them. The powerDependent multiplier converts it to a LIFE-SUPPORTING device (oxygen concentrator, which is over 99% of that group; ventilator; home dialysis). Assumed energy: CPAP 90 Wh a night without humidifier and 220-350 Wh with; life-supporting 1,500 Wh a day as a blend (portable concentrator or ventilator about 500-1,000; stationary 5 L concentrator about 7,000).

baselineCoverageDays.basis: Portable concentrator batteries last 2-4 h and up to 12 h with external packs at the lowest setting (Molinari et al. 2017, https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/41187); an E cylinder holds about 680 L, 5.7 h at 2 L/min (recalled). In the 2003 blackout 23 of 255 patients at one New York emergency department within 24 h came for device failure (Greenwald 2004, search snippet). CPAP has no backup, so its coverage is 0.

hardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: CPAP-class user: a night of broken sleep, sleepiness and headache, worsening as sleep debt builds. Lower bound is what users already pay for the therapy, a few dollars a night. No WTP study found.

mortalityMicromortsPerPersonDay.basis: CPAP-class user. Upper bound from observational data: untreated severe sleep apnoea had 0.7 more fatal cardiovascular events per 100 person-years than CPAP-treated (Marin 2005, recalled) = 19 micromorts a day; randomised trials found no mortality benefit. Drowsy driving adds under 1. Chosen so that base x 100 reproduces the life-supporting estimate, which is the number with evidence behind it.

multipliers.basis: Life-supporting device: 200 micromorts a day (30-1,500) on days 1-2 and 300 (50-2,000) from day 3; hardship $300 a day. (a) NOTT: 12-month mortality 20.6% on nocturnal-only oxygen against 11.9% on continuous (https://www.wikijournalclub.org/wiki/NOTT) = 8.7 points a year = 238 micromorts a day for patients with severe resting hypoxaemia. (b) Texas 2021: 25 deaths from exacerbated illness, 8 respiratory and 6 renal (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf), say 8-15 from loss of device power, among roughly 200,000 device users of whom 69% lost power for a mean 42 h (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf) = 33-62 micromorts per outage day on the official count, about three times that on excess-death counts, and with many users relocating. (c) Irma: 3 oxygen-dependent deaths (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/mm6730a5.htm), an order of magnitude lower, after relocation and resupply. Hardship x15 ($300 a day) is a guess for breathlessness, fear and confinement; no WTP data found.

needs.notes: Do not stack age multipliers: the anchors already reflect the age of real device users. Ventilator-dependent people (under 1% of the group, Molinari) face death within hours once the internal battery (typically 4-8 h, recalled) is gone; their risk per unmet day is plausibly 10,000-500,000 micromorts and the group average must not be read as applying to them. Home haemodialysis and cycler peritoneal dialysis tolerate a day or two; peritoneal patients can switch to manual exchanges. About 14.5M US households (11%) have a medical device that needs electricity (AHS 2023, https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/10/power-outages.html); roughly 685,000 people were on a ventilator or concentrator at home in 2012 (Molinari) and about 3 million Medicare beneficiaries are on the wider HHS emPOWER list (search snippet).

effects.amountUnit: Wh-equivalent (about half a day of oxygen at the blended 1,500 Wh a day; two E cylinders give 11 h at 2 L/min continuous, several times that with a conserver)
effects.notes: Oxygen users only; does nothing for ventilators or dialysis.

fractionRemoved.basis: Leaving early for a powered place, before the backup runs out, removes the unmet days that follow; the share is my judgement.

adherence.basis: People delay leaving; 18% of Texans left home in 2021 (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf).

effects.notes: Acts through relocation; the engine should not also credit the same days to the leave option.

evidence.claim: Insurance claims identified electricity-dependent people with 93% accuracy but fewer than 2.5% were on the local special-needs registry
In the 2003 blackout 23 of 255 patients at one emergency department in 24 h came for device failure, 19 of them oxygen equipment; 13 were admitted

items.notes: Added candidate. Almost free, so it should rank above every battery for oxygen users, but its effect sizes are judgement.

items.name: Frozen water bottles and fridge thermometers
items.spec: Two appliance thermometers (fridge and freezer) and 4-6 one-litre bottles of water kept frozen in spare freezer space; in an outage move some to the fridge and keep doors shut.

usdPerUnit.basis: Taylor 5924 dial fridge/freezer thermometer $3.69 each, read on https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/refrigerator-freezer-thermometer.html; two = $7.38. Bottles are reused.

setupHours.basis: Fill and freeze bottles; place thermometers.

everydayShare.basis: Thermometers catch a warm fridge in normal times.

reliability.basis: Bottles get evicted when the freezer fills.

effects.notes: 5 kg of ice absorbs 464 Wh of heat (334 kJ/kg); a closed fridge compartment gains roughly 30 W (my estimate from 1.2 kWh a day of consumption), so about 15 h. CDC: a full freezer holds 48 h against 24 h half-full.

effects.description: The thermometer shows whether food stayed at or below 40F, so safe food is kept and unsafe food discarded; 65% of people judge by smell (RTI 2011). Not separately quantified.

evidence.claim: Fridge safe 4 h, full freezer 48 h, half-full 24 h; frozen containers of water help keep food at or below 40F
Only about a third knew to discard refrigerated perishables after 4 h; 65% smelled food to judge safety
4.9M households reported spoiled food from outages in 2023

items.notes: Helps only in outages of roughly 10 h to 2 days; beyond that everything is lost regardless. A cooler and bought ice do the same job late.

excluded.reason: Flame light with stored liquid fuel; dominated by LED lights and folded into the candles note.

openQuestions: medicalPower: the schema asks for a curve for a healthy adult, who has no device. I set the base curve for an important-device user (CPAP class) and the powerDependent multiplier for life support. The engine must apply the need only to people flagged as device users. There is no flag for the 11% of households with a non-life-supporting device; suggest a profile and condition medicalDevice.
Households with a car have chargePhone at baseline. Either give devicePower a baseline of weeks when condition car holds, or charge car households only an inconvenience cost of about $2-3 a day.

Watt-hour stocks are shared across devicePower, light, refrigeration and medicalPower. The engine needs a priority order (medical, then phones and light, then fridge) and must not add the same Wh to several needs.

mainsPower needs a wattage: 150 W (car inverter), 300 W (small power station), 1,500 W or more (1 kWh station, generator). Only the last starts a fridge, and only the generator has the energy for heating or cooling.
A met/unmet light need gives all the value to the first lamp. Suggest: the first light capability removes 70-80% of light hardship and one light per two people removes the rest.
devicePower should be charged only when the comms window is not active, and refrigeration should be waived in cold events (coldShare) because food can go outside.
Ventilator-dependent people are under 1% of powerDependent but carry risks 100 to 1,000 times the group mean; the published list should say the life-support figures describe oxygen users.

Acute risk of a few days without supplemental oxygen is inferred from year-long trials and three event counts; no cohort study of device users in outages was found. This is the number most worth better evidence.
